audio_caption: The audio clip begins with a male speaker introducing a topic. He mentions that they will be looking at "old, lost, and forgotten techniques" released by a specific group and promises to provide a link in the description. He suggests that the techniques are "something a little bit new" or variations of existing techniques, which could be surprising in competition. The speaker then defines the title as "lost techniques" and "forgotten techniques".

The audio clip begins with a male speaker introducing "Seoi Otoshi" as the first technique to be discussed, referring to a 1928 image. He describes the movement, emphasizing the arm hook and waist grab for the opponent's belt, explaining that the technique is a cutting motion down. The speaker clarifies that there's some back loading involved, then mentions the use of the sleeve and belt grips.

A male speaker discusses a wrestling technique using terms such as "grip will create a great assist to the arm", "cutting on the lapel and the arm", and "sudden explosiveness". He compares different variations of the throw, emphasizing positioning and how that can determine the type of throw. The speaker's tone is informative and analytical. He continues describing wrestling techniques, suggesting something could be added to an arsenal.
The audio clip contains speech from a male speaker, possibly introducing a person named "Suri Otoshi". His tone is informative and deliberate.

The audio clip features a single male speaker discussing a specific technique, mentioning its connection to others and providing a physical description. His tone is conversational, somewhat academic, focusing on the details and comparisons. The description of a technique is followed by another named “Yokowakare,” with the speaker indicating a future comparison.

The clip starts with a male speaker introducing the next topic, "O-Yoko-Wakari or Major Side Separation." He describes the move, comparing it to a foot sweep, noting that you place the sole of your foot on the side at ankle level, "kind of like Yokogake," and use your arms to take them sideways. He suggests this might be a variation of Yokogake, where, in Yokogake, the arm movement is minimal, unlike here. He continues, describing the basic form, emphasizing the lift and throw, and the dropping of weight with hands doing the work, then comparing this form to blocking feet sideways and using your arms to hurl.

The clip opens with a single male speaker beginning to describe "a competition example." He notes the "Mongolian judoka," and describes her technique as "brilliant." The speaker describes the opponent flattening herself to the side and taking her down using the sleeve only, noting how some might consider a basic version as ineffective, while suggesting it is truly effective.  He then describes another technique, identifying it as "yoko wakare." He contrasts this technique to the first, referencing blocking and using the sleeve to push, sacrificing oneself to the side in "yoko gake." He makes further distinctions, explaining that it's different and similar to other techniques, discussing how to "block the foot" as if attempting a sweep.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker introducing a judo technique called "Yoko-Gake" and comparing it to its variant, "O Yoko-Wakare." He describes the technique, highlighting the slapping of the ankle with the foot and pushing the sleeve to the side. Then, he explains how it is more effective when done with a strong pull, differentiating this from just pushing the sleeve towards the ribs, and compares it to Sasae. He continues, noting the technique can also be used as O Yoko-Wakare, and mentions various grips like overhooks and underhooks. He concludes by stating that the technique is easy to execute without a Gi.

A male speaker introduces the final topic, "knee on belly in Judo," stating it might seem obvious but is a debated technique. He refers to a 1929 picture, naming Oda Tsunetane as the author and describing a knee on the solar plexus visible in the image. He then mentions another picture from the side offering a better view.

The audio clip features a single male speaker who seems to be instructing or explaining something. He starts discussing "Uki Gatame" and mentions it's used differently nowadays like an "S mount" in Jujutsu. He continues, explaining that the basic form, particularly when using a crossface, can lead to quick submissions due to its effectiveness as a strangle if properly executed. He emphasizes that someone won't last long if the technique is done correctly and includes pulling the sleeves while applying pressure to the knee and solar plexus. Finally, he reaffirms that this technique is known as "Uki Gatame" today.
The clip contains a single male speaker discussing armbars and jujutsu techniques like "S mount". He describes it as a "floating hold" and uses the term "neon belly" with an informative tone.

The audio clip features one male speaker who encourages listeners to add comments below and to check a link to an article. He describes the article as "big" and mentions it includes information about the All-Japan competition, suggesting listeners take their time reading and enjoying the pictures. He expresses gratitude to the listeners before concluding.
